question: A wound is described as having irregular, torn edges with tissue bridges visible across the wound floor, no hair bulbs at the wound margins, and underlying subcutaneous bruising. Which wound type is this?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lacerations are produced by blunt force that tears rather than cuts tissue. The hallmark features are: irregular margins, tissue bridges (nerves, blood vessels, connective tissue) crossing the wound base, no hair bulb transection at margins (hair is torn, not cut), and bruising of the wound margins and underlying tissue.

Incorrect. Incised wounds (produced by sharp-edged weapons) have clean, regular, sharply defined edges, no tissue bridges, and hair bulbs are cut cleanly at the margins. Irregular edges and tissue bridges indicate blunt tearing — a laceration.

Incorrect. An abrasion involves only the epidermis — it is a superficial graze without a wound floor of the depth described. Abrasions do not show tissue bridges; they show removal or compression of superficial skin layers.

Incorrect. A stab wound is produced by a pointed weapon and is characterised by depth greater than surface length, usually with clean entry wound margins. Irregular edges and tissue bridges point to blunt tearing, not stabbing.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key discriminator is tissue bridges: blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue that remain intact across the wound base after blunt tearing. These are NEVER present in incised wounds and are the primary sign of a laceration.
Correct. Tissue bridges are the single most reliable distinguishing feature of a laceration versus an incised wound — their presence confirms blunt tearing rather than sharp cutting.
